objective: Performing qualitative analysis: classifying risks in an RBS, applying risk matrices, and prioritizing by impact/urgency

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the risk manager for a fictional stadium roof replacement for Harbor City. The register has 90 risks, each scored differently by whoever raised it.
handover: Scores range from 'high-ish' to '7/10'; there is no shared scale.
The roof must be weathertight before the season opens in 30 weeks.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: a deleted crane-access risk materializes; the lift is delayed two weeks.
Week 3: the sponsor's ranking skips the roofing membrane supply risk; the supplier's delay hits.
Week 4: the steel order deadline passes unnoticed among thirty 'top' risks; fabrication slips five weeks.

rbsPrompt.title: An unstructured register
rbsPrompt.context: Duplicates and gaps are hard to see.

choices.label: Classify every risk in a risk breakdown structure (technical, external, organizational, project management), merge duplicates and look for empty branches

effects.log: 62 risks remain; weather and permitting gaps surface.

choices.feedback: An RBS groups risks by source, exposing duplicates, concentrations and gaps.

choices.label: Sort the register alphabetically
choices.feedback: Order without structure; duplicates and gaps remain.

choices.label: Keep the 20 risks with the highest scores and delete the rest
choices.feedback: The scores use four scales; real risks are deleted.

matrixPrompt.title: Four scoring scales
matrixPrompt.context: Owners score risks their own way.

choices.label: Re-score all 62 risks in a workshop on the plan's 5x5 matrix with its definitions of probability and impact, calibrated with two worked examples
choices.feedback: A risk matrix with agreed definitions makes scores comparable across owners.

choices.label: Average the four scales into one number
choices.feedback: Mixing scales produces numbers that mean nothing.

choices.label: Let the sponsor rank them by feel
choices.feedback: One person's view replaces the team's analysis.

urgencyPrompt.title: Equal scores, different timing
urgencyPrompt.context: Several risks score the same; some must be acted on this month.

choices.label: Add urgency (time until a response must start) and put high-score risks needing action within six weeks at the top, with owners and response dates

effects.log: The top ten are clear, with dates.

choices.feedback: Urgency separates equal scores: risks whose response window is closing come first.

choices.label: Prioritize by score alone
choices.feedback: A late-season risk outranks one whose window closes next week.

choices.label: Mark every red risk as top priority
choices.feedback: With thirty top priorities, none gets attention.

reflection.question: Write the qualitative risk analysis record for the sponsor.

parts.label: Structure and scores
parts.criteria: RBS; 62 risks on the agreed 5x5 matrix.
parts.modelAnswer: We classified the register in an RBS, merged 28 duplicates and re-scored the remaining 62 on the plan's matrix.

parts.label: Priorities
parts.criteria: Top ten by score and urgency, with owners and dates.
parts.modelAnswer: The top ten combine high scores with response windows inside six weeks; each has an owner and a response date.
